chapter_theme: ஒப்புரவு is the obligation to make one's means serve the community, expecting nothing back as rain expects nothing. It is treated as the mark of being alive, and it holds even in poverty and at the cost of ruin.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of ஒப்புரவு (211-213), then 214 on not failing in it, how the wealth of such a person serves others (215-217), why poverty doesn't release one from it (218-219), and why loss through it is no loss (220).

211.reading: Obligation seeks no return: what does the world do for the rain in exchange?
211.nuance: The word chosen is கடப்பாடு, what is owed, and not gift. Parimelazhagar points out that the name itself implies it can't be dropped. Giving with no return is therefore framed as debt, a nicely paradoxical idea.

212.reading: All the wealth got through exertion exists for doing வேளாண்மை, with தக்கார் standing in some relation to it.
212.nuance: The grammar of தக்கார்க்கு decides whether this sets a limit on recipients or describes the owner, so I have left it open in the reading.

positions.position: தக்கார் are the owners: for those who are worthy, all wealth is for benevolence, not for private consumption or hoarding.
தக்கார் are the recipients: the wealth is for helping those who deserve it.
positions.quote: ஒருவன் முயன்று ஈட்டிய பொருளெல்லாம் தகுதியுடையார்க்கு உபகரித்தற்காகவாம்

213.reading: Whether in the world of புத்தேள் or here, it is hard to find any other thing as good as ஒப்புரவு.
213.nuance: Parimelazhagar offers a striking reason for the gods' world: all there are alike, with no giver and no receiver, so this good can't exist there. On that view the human condition of need is what makes the highest good possible.

positions.position: புத்தேள் உலகு is the world of the gods.
It is a new world yet to come, which removes the gods from the verse.

214.reading: One who knows what is fitting truly lives; anyone else is counted among the dead.
214.nuance: Knowing here includes doing: Parimelazhagar glosses it as knowing and acting, because the dead neither know nor act.

positions.position: What is fitting is the way of the world as a whole, and lapses in it can't be repaired as lapses in Vedic practice can.
positions.quote: உலகநடை வழு வேதநடை வழுப்போலத் தீர்திறன் உடைத்து அன்று

positions.position: What is fitting is specifically ஒப்புரவு, and those who lack it are like corpses.

215.reading: The wealth of a greatly wise person connected with the world's desiring is like water filling the village's drinking tank.
215.nuance: The image puts the wealth in a common place, and the owner disappears from the picture: people simply draw from it. This verse calls such a person பேரறிவாளன, wise, not merely generous.

positions.position: This person desires and practises the world's way.
positions.quote: உலகநடையை விரும்பிச் செய்யும் பெரிய அறிவினை யுடையவனது செல்வம்

positions.position: This person is the one desired by all the world.

216.reading: Wealth falling to one who has நயன் is like a fruit-giving tree ripening in the heart of the town.
216.nuance: Parimelazhagar says that நயன் here is ஒப்புரவு as the chief of worldly justice, Manakkudavar makes it being loved by others, and Kalaignar a tender heart. The tree's public position matters as much as its fruit, since no one has to go looking for it.

217.reading: Wealth falling to one of great nobility is like a tree that is medicine and never fails.
217.nuance: This goes further than the fruit tree of 216. Parimelazhagar has every part of the tree serving as cure, with no regard for its own lack, which suggests giving that costs the giver something. He and Manakkudavar agree that தப்பா includes never being hidden from those who seek it.

218.reading: Even at a time without means, those whose sight knows what is due don't falter in ஒப்புரவு.
218.nuance: The verse cuts ஒப்புரவு free from wealth. If it were a by-product of surplus it would lapse with the surplus.

219.reading: Poverty, for one with நயன், is just the condition of being unable to rest while what should be done goes undone.
219.nuance: Poverty is redefined from the inside. Parimelazhagar makes the contrast explicit: it isn't going without one's own enjoyments. The deprivation is of the power to give.

220.reading: If ruin is said to come through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth acquiring even by selling oneself.
220.nuance: The verse deals with an objection: 'if it is said'. For Parimelazhagar nothing is normally worth selling oneself for, so this is meant to startle, and the reason he gives is the fame such loss yields.

positions.position: Selling oneself is meant literally as the limit case: the loss is worth buying even at that price.
positions.quote: அக்கேடு தன்னை விற்றாயினும் கொள்ளும் தகுதியை உடைத்து.

positions.position: It is a commercial image, selling one thing to obtain another, so the 'loss' is really a trade for later benefit.
positions.quote: ஒன்றை விற்று ஒன்றைக் கொள்ளுகின்ற வாணிகமாகக் கொள்ளுந் தகுதி புடைத்து

links.note: 211 insists that obligation looks for no return. 226 commends feeding the destitute as the place to store one's wealth, and Parimelazhagar says it comes back to help the giver. One motive disclaims reward and the other promises it.

An exact inversion: the same tree in mid-town, same ripening. In 216 it bears useful fruit; in 1008 it is a poison tree. The chapters on benevolence and on useless wealth share one picture, and only the owner's character changes it.
Both move the definition of being alive from body to relationship: 80 to love, 214 to knowing what is due. The body without these is bone and skin, or a corpse.
219 says the good man's poverty is being unable to give. 230 pushes this further: being unable to give makes even death sweet.
220 only says that ruin from generosity is worth buying. 235 takes up the same word and explains how there can be a ruin that is a gain, and says that only the skilled achieve it.

source_issues: 214: the verse text reads ஒத்த தறவோன், while Parimelazhagar's gloss (ஒத்தது அறிவான்) and Pope's rendering point to the reading ஒத்த தறிவான். The readings here follow the commentators.
212: Parimelazhagar's text contains a stray character in எல்‘ம், evidently எல்லாம்.
220: Manakkudavar's text has the likely typo அஃறு for அஃது.
